body:
What are literary sources?

Literary sources are written or orally transmitted works that preserve information about the ideas, beliefs, institutions and experiences of the past. They include religious compositions, poems, stories, political treatises, biographies and historical chronicles.

Some literary works were composed long before the surviving copies were written. This distinction is especially important when studying ancient Indian texts.

Manuscripts and inscriptions are not the same

A manuscript is a text written by hand. In ancient and medieval India, manuscripts were commonly prepared on materials such as palm leaves and birch bark. Other writing materials, including paper, were used in later periods.

By contrast, an inscription is writing recorded on a surface such as stone or metal. Both can contain valuable historical information, but they differ in their physical form and typical uses.

Why the date of a manuscript matters

A manuscript copied in the 11th century CE might contain a work composed much earlier. Its physical date therefore does not necessarily indicate when the original ideas were first expressed.

Because manuscripts were copied by hand, differences could arise between copies. The existence of several versions of a text should not automatically be taken to mean that they were written by different original authors.

Major types of literary evidence

Vedic literature

The Rigveda is among the oldest known Sanskrit compositions. Its hymns were composed and transmitted orally during the 2nd millennium BCE.

Vedic literature is important for understanding religious ideas and aspects of the society in which its traditions developed. It should not be treated as a complete record of every community living in the subcontinent at that time.

Buddhist and Jain literature

Buddhist and Jain literary traditions contain teachings, stories, rules and accounts associated with religious communities. The Buddhist Tripitaka and Jain Agamas are important examples.

Such works help in studying religious thought and social ideas. The historical value of a particular account depends on its nature and the period to which it refers.

Tamil Sangam literature

Sangam literature consists of early Tamil compositions. It is useful for understanding aspects of society, chiefs, exchange and cultural life in ancient south India.

Poems may preserve information about real places and political figures, but poetic descriptions must be distinguished from literal records of events.

Political treatises and accounts

The Arthashastra is a major Sanskrit work associated with political organisation, administration and economic matters. It is traditionally connected with Kautilya or Chanakya.

The work is relevant to discussions of ancient Indian political ideas. Its prescriptions describe arrangements or practices advocated in the text; they should not automatically be treated as evidence that every ruler followed them in exactly the same manner.

Chronicles and biographies

Chronicles may describe rulers, events and political developments in chronological order. Biographies generally focus on the life of a particular person.

Kalhana, writing in the 12th century CE, composed the Rajatarangini, an account of the rulers of Kashmir. His work drew upon earlier historical materials, including inscriptions and written records.

What literary sources can establish

Literary sources are particularly useful for understanding beliefs, ideas, cultural practices and how authors represented their societies. When a text describes a ruler's victory or an event from an earlier century, other sources may be needed to confirm the historical details.

Manuscript identifies a handwritten physical text. Literary source identifies the content and its use as evidence. A religious composition can survive in manuscript form without having been originally composed on that manuscript.

Prelims focus

  • Manuscripts were commonly written on palm leaves and birch bark.
  • The Rigveda is an early Sanskrit composition associated with Vedic traditions.
  • The Tripitaka is associated with Buddhism; the Agamas are associated with Jainism.
  • Sangam literature is an important source for early Tamil society.
  • The Arthashastra is traditionally associated with Kautilya or Chanakya.
  • Trap: The date of a surviving manuscript copy is not necessarily the date when the work was originally composed.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 1, pp. 4–5, and Chapter 5, What Books and Burials Tell Us; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 1, pp. 4–6, and Chapter 2, pp. 18–20; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 32–33 and 35–39.]

title: Manuscripts, Religious Texts and Historical Chronicles

body:
Why are travellers' accounts useful?

Travellers sometimes recorded what they observed during journeys across the Indian subcontinent. Their descriptions can provide information about cities, religious institutions, trade routes, customs, administration and everyday life.

Such accounts are valuable because visitors sometimes described practices that local writers regarded as ordinary and did not record. However, a traveller's experience was limited to the places visited, the people encountered and the subjects that interested the author.

Important travellers and associated works

TravellerBroad periodImportant association
Megasthenes4th–3rd centuries BCEGreek ambassador at Chandragupta Maurya's court; Indica
Fa Xian5th century CEChinese Buddhist pilgrim; Buddhist sites and monasteries
Xuan Zang7th century CEChinese Buddhist pilgrim; monasteries and Nalanda
Al-Biruni11th century CEKitab-ul-Hind, written in Arabic
Ibn Battuta14th century CEMoroccan traveller; Rihla, written in Arabic

Megasthenes and Mauryan India

Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador associated with the court of Chandragupta Maurya. His account, commonly known as Indica, is an important source for discussions of Mauryan India.

The original work does not survive as a complete text. Information attributed to it is preserved through later writers. This is important when distinguishing the original traveller's account from the form in which it is available today.

Chinese Buddhist pilgrims

Fa Xian

Fa Xian, a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim who travelled in India during the 5th century CE, visited places associated with Buddhism. His account is useful for studying religious institutions and aspects of life during his travels.

Xuan Zang

Xuan Zang visited India during the 7th century CE. His descriptions of Buddhist institutions, including Nalanda in present-day Bihar, are valuable sources for the study of education and Buddhism in that period.

These 2 travellers belong to different centuries. They should not be treated as contemporaries.

Al-Biruni and the Kitab-ul-Hind

Al-Biruni was a scholar from Khwarizm, in present-day Uzbekistan, who studied India during the 11th century CE.

His Kitab-ul-Hind was written in Arabic. It describes subjects including religion, philosophy, customs, social life, astronomy and systems of measurement. Al-Biruni drew upon his knowledge of Sanskrit texts and discussions with scholars.

The work is a major source for understanding how an educated visitor investigated and described Indian society in his time.

Ibn Battuta and the Rihla

Ibn Battuta was a traveller from Morocco who visited India during the 14th century CE, in the period of the Delhi Sultanate.

His account, known as the Rihla, was written in Arabic. It contains observations about travel, cities, people, institutions and other aspects of society.

Ibn Battuta belongs to a later medieval period than Al-Biruni. Their accounts should not be assigned to the same century merely because both wrote in Arabic.

How to understand a traveller's evidence

A traveller's account must be connected to the period and place actually described. An eyewitness description may provide valuable evidence about a particular institution. It does not establish that the same conditions existed throughout India.

The traveller's purpose also matters. Buddhist pilgrims were especially interested in Buddhist sites and institutions, while an ambassador might record matters relevant to government or court life. Different interests produced different kinds of evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Megasthenes was associated with Chandragupta Maurya; his work was called Indica.
  • Fa Xian visited India in the 5th century CE.
  • Xuan Zang visited in the 7th century CE and described Nalanda.
  • Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic during the 11th century CE.
  • Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan traveller of the 14th century CE, is associated with the Arabic Rihla.
  • Trap: A traveller's description of 1 place should not be assumed to describe the entire subcontinent.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 32–33; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 10, Traders, Kings and Pilgrims, pp. 105–106; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 2, p. 21; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 5, Through the Eyes of Travellers, pp. 115–119.]

pictures.caption: A traveller's observations are strongest for the places and activities actually described.

title: Foreign Travellers and Their Accounts of India

body:
Match the historical claim with the evidence it requires

Historical sources become useful when they are connected to a clearly stated claim. A question about the physical structure of a settlement usually requires material evidence. A question about the wording of a ruler's order requires a written record. A question about coinage requires evidence from coins.

Several sources may contribute to the same conclusion. They do not necessarily provide identical information, and 1 source should not be made to prove more than it records.

Evidence-based examples

Historical claimMost relevant evidenceImportant distinction
Mohenjodaro had a drainage system.Remains of drains and buildingsPhysical structures establish the arrangement, not the ruler's identity.
Dholavira stored water.Reservoirs and water-management structuresMaterial remains support water-storage arrangements.
Ashoka issued public messages about dhamma.Rock and pillar inscriptionsThe record establishes the message, not universal obedience to it.
Rudradaman recorded repairs to Sudarshana Lake.Junagadh inscription of 150 CEThe inscription is Sanskrit written in Brahmi script.
Punch-marked coinage existed in early historic India.Punch-marked silver and copper coinsCoinage provides monetary evidence, not complete political boundaries.
Buddhist pilgrims visited Indian monasteries.Accounts of Fa Xian and Xuan ZangTheir journeys occurred in different centuries.
Early medieval rulers granted land.Copper-plate grantsThe grant records an entitlement; a prashasti primarily praises its patron.

Distinguishing similar-looking sources

Stone inscription and stone tool

A stone inscription contains deliberately recorded writing. A stone tool provides material evidence about an activity. The fact that both are made of stone does not make them the same kind of source.

Coin and seal

A coin is associated with monetary use. A seal can carry symbols or writing and may be relevant to identification or exchange, but it is not automatically a coin.

Manuscript and inscription

A manuscript is handwritten on a writing material such as palm leaf, birch bark or paper. An inscription is recorded on a surface such as stone or metal. Both can preserve written information.

Prashasti and land grant

A prashasti praises a ruler or patron. A land-grant inscription records the grant of land or associated rights. A single inscription can contain both praise and a record of a grant, but the 2 functions should be distinguished.

Chronology must agree with the source

The approximate date of the source should be compatible with the event being studied. Ashoka's inscriptions belong to the 3rd century BCE, while Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription dates to 150 CE. They cannot both be contemporary records of the same ruler's reign.

Similarly, Fa Xian belongs to the 5th century CE, Xuan Zang to the 7th century CE, Al-Biruni to the 11th century CE and Ibn Battuta to the 14th century CE. Associating a traveller with the wrong century produces an incorrect historical pairing.

One-glance revision of chronology and sources

The most important distinction is between what the evidence directly records or preserves and what is inferred from it. Harappan drains directly preserve construction features; their layout supports conclusions about urban planning. Ashokan inscriptions preserve royal messages; they support conclusions about what Ashoka proclaimed. Coins preserve material and written features associated with exchange and authority; they do not automatically establish the boundaries of a kingdom.

Use the correct historical relationship

  • Chronology: identifies when an event or development occurred.
  • Archaeology: provides material evidence of human activity.
  • Epigraphy: provides evidence from inscriptions.
  • Numismatics: provides evidence from coins.
  • Literary and travellers' accounts: preserve descriptions, ideas and observations that must be read in their historical context.

Prelims focus

  • Mature Harappan: approximately 2600–1900 BCE; script remains undeciphered.
  • Ashoka: 3rd century BCE; inscriptions are major contemporary sources.
  • Rudradaman: Junagadh inscription, 150 CE; Sanskrit language, Brahmi script.
  • Gupta rulers: important sources include coins and inscriptions.
  • Early medieval India: copper-plate grants, inscriptions and manuscripts are important sources.
  • Trap: A source can establish that a claim was recorded without proving that every part of the claim was historically accurate.

[Sources: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 66–68; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Themes 1–2, pp. 1–9 and 28–49; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 2, pp. 18–20; Archaeological Survey of India, Bharat SHRI, Photo Gallery, Brahmi Inscription of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman from Junagadh, consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Historical questions require both a suitable date and a suitable source.

title: Choosing the Correct Historical Source and Interpreting Evidence
